intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that multiple epiphyseal dysplasia-2 (EDM2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding the alpha-2 chain of type IX collagen (COL9A2) on chromosome 1p32.3-p33.

checks.evidence_quote: Together with previous reports our results indicate that mutations leading to skipping of exon 3 within the COL3 domain of the alpha2-chain of collagen type IX may be relatively common in patients with a special subtype of multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED) in which the hips are not markedly affected at early age (EDM2).
checks.explanation: The abstract links COL9A2 mutation to EDM2. It does not state the zygosity (heterozygous).

paragraphs.text: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED) is a dominantly inherited chondrodysplasia characterized by mild short stature and early-onset osteoarthrosis (Briggs et al., 1994). The EDM2 subtype has been described as a form of MED in which the hips are not markedly affected at an early age, with childhood onset of pain and stiffness of the knees, ankles, elbows, and finger joints, free articular bodies, and early degenerative joint disease (Fiedler et al., 2002).

paragraphs.text: Versteylen et al. (1988) described 2 families that appeared to contain examples of multiple epiphyseal dysplasia. In both families there was a striking incidence of severe osteochondritis of the knees, which the authors suggested was caused by the fragmented and maldeveloped epiphyses characteristic of epiphyseal dysplasia. The molecular basis in these families was not reported in the abstract.

paragraphs.text: Fiedler et al. (2002) reported a family of 19 individuals over 4 generations in which 12 members were affected with a variant of multiple epiphyseal dysplasia. Beginning in childhood, the disease led to pain and stiffness of the knees, ankles, elbows, and finger joints. Some adult patients repeatedly suffered from free articular bodies resulting in locking of the joint, and affected individuals were prone to the development of early degenerative joint disease. Electron microscopy showed that the diameter of collagen fibrils from arthroscopically removed free articular bodies of 2 patients was not obviously different from that of normal articular cartilage. The authors noted that in this subtype of MED the hips are not markedly affected at an early age.

paragraphs.text: In a 4-generation family with EDM2, Fiedler et al. (2002) identified a G-C substitution at position -1 of the COL9A2 exon 3/intron 3 splicing region by mutation screening of candidate regions; the authors stated that it most probably alters splicing. Family screening by automated sequencing and BsaWI digestion of amplicons confirmed the substitution in 8 clinically affected family members and in 3 presymptomatic young children. Together with previous reports, the authors concluded that mutations leading to skipping of exon 3 within the COL3 domain of the alpha-2 chain of collagen IX may be relatively common in patients with this subtype of MED.

agent.process_note: I opened all 7 files. None had full text: 4 had abstracts only (Versteylen 1988, Warman 1994, Briggs 1994, Fiedler 2002) and 3 had titles only (Barrie 1958, Muragaki 1996, Nakashima 2005). I could not cite Barrie 1958 or Nakashima 2005 for anything specific, so I left them out. Muragaki 1996 is cited only for what its title says (a COL9A2 mutation causes EDM2); its variant, family details and methods were not available. Fiedler's abstract gives no numbered nucleotide or protein change, only a G-C at position -1 of the exon 3/intron 3 splice region, so HGVS is left empty. No HGNC data was supplied, so no gene MIM number is given. I took the 1p32.3-p33 location from Warman 1994. Zygosity is never stated outright. I wrote 'heterozygous' based on dominant inheritance (Briggs) and a 4-generation family (Fiedler).
